article_title: Ladders to Literacy
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2007). Ladders to Literacy for Kindergarten Students. WWC Intervention Report. https://www.brookespublishing.com
title: Supplemental literacy activities designed for low preparation and integration into existing classroom routines
description: The curriculum's activity format embeds supplemental skill work into ordinary classroom life. "Typically the teacher chooses activities that can be included in the current classroom routines and that require little preparation time." Most activities are designed for large groups, follow a similar format, and can be scheduled weekly, monthly, or one time; oral language activities cross-reference other sections to encourage integration across skills.
requirements: A teacher able to select activities matching current classroom routines, keeping preparation time low.
constraints: The pattern is described for the supplemental kindergarten curriculum context; the WWC evaluated it as part of the whole program rather than in isolation.
target_learners: kindergarten students in large-group classroom settings
target_learning_goals: print awareness
phonological awareness
oral language
examples: Intervention teachers delivered activities such as sound isolation, first sounds, rhyming, invented spelling, story grammar, and integrating spelling and reading within existing classroom routines.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2007). Ladders to Literacy for Kindergarten Students. WWC Intervention Report. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/259

article_title: Lovaas Model of Applied Behavior Analysis
citation: Lovaas Model of Applied Behavior Analysis. (2010). WWC Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Staged progression from discrete trial training to naturalistic instruction and generalization
description: The Lovaas Model organizes instruction as a staged progression. "During the first stages of the intervention, the main method of teaching is discrete trial training", and "As children progress, therapists gradually increase the emphasis on instruction in less structured or more natural settings, such as peer play and classrooms." Early stages target reducing behaviors that interfere with learning and teaching prerequisite skills such as requesting, imitation, and following instructions; instruction then advances to expressive and receptive language, then social and conversation skills, and finally pre-academic and observational learning skills, with programming for generalization to preschool and community settings.
requirements: Trained one-to-one instructors, trainers, and supervisors delivering 35 to 40 hours per week of intervention
constraints: The intervention generally lasts about three years, beginning with children ages 18 to 42 months
target_learners: young children with autism or pervasive developmental disorder
target_learning_goals: prerequisite skills such as requesting and imitation
expressive and receptive language
social and conversation skills
pre-academic skills and generalization
examples: A typical therapy session lasts two to three hours, with structured time devoted to tasks such as appropriate toy play or following instructions, followed by breaks used for incidental teaching or generalization activities
key_sources: Lovaas Model of Applied Behavior Analysis. (2010). WWC Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/295

article_title: Catapult Learning's Educational Services
citation: Catapult Learning's Wraparound Supplemental Educational Services. (2024). Evidence review, program description and outcomes. https://www.catapultlearning.com
title: Deliver supplemental academic services in a structured environment with a low student-to-teacher ratio
description: The Wraparound program is delivered in a structured environment with a low student-to-teacher ratio, which the page presents as part of how the program aims to accelerate academic achievement while fostering a supportive learning atmosphere. Staffing criteria by service type (certified instructors, certified counselors, experienced coaches) support this delivery model.
requirements: Instructors with state-compliant certification; counselors with certification and/or MSW; coaches with 2 years of K-8 experience
constraints: No required technology component to the program model or the delivery of services
target_learners: K-12 students receiving supplemental educational services
target_learning_goals: Accelerated academic achievement in literacy and math
examples: The evaluated program model paired small-group AchieveMath and AchieveLiteracy instruction with counseling and special education support in a parochial school district

article_title: City Studies: Project Meta-Analysis
citation: Margaret E. Raymond, Won Fy Lee. (2022). City Studies Project Meta-Analysis by CREDO of Stanford University: Cohort 1 Cities. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Stanford University. https://credo.stanford.edu/city-studies/
title: Locally driven solutions and implementation flexibility may be necessary conditions for successful student learning
description: Drawing on the heterogeneous city-level growth patterns in the meta-analysis, the report's discussion proposes that effective learning practices are highly localized rather than a single uniform solution. It states that "schools' ability to ﬁnd locally driven solutions to the locally identiﬁed problems and to allow ﬂexibility in implementing a proposed set of remedies could be necessary conditions for successful student learning." The principle frames school-level autonomy and local problem identification as design conditions for improving learning growth in urban school systems.
requirements: Schools must have the ability to identify problems locally and devise locally driven solutions
Flexibility in implementing a proposed set of remedies
constraints: The report presents this as an interpretation of observed heterogeneous trends, not a tested manipulation; it is stated as a possibility ("could be necessary conditions")
target_learners: K-12 public school students in urban districts, mainly low-income and minority students
target_learning_goals: Academic performance growth in reading and mathematics
examples: The report's discussion links the positive charter contributions across heterogeneous city trends to locally driven solutions and implementation flexibility
key_sources: Margaret E. Raymond, Won Fy Lee. (2022). City Studies Project Meta-Analysis by CREDO of Stanford University: Cohort 1 Cities. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Stanford University. https://credo.stanford.edu/city-studies/

article_title: Longitudinal Models of Reading and Mathematics Achievement in Deaf and Hard of Hearing Students
citation: Stephanie Cawthon, Johny Daniel, North Cooc, Ana Vielma. (2022). Longitudinal models of reading and mathematics achievement in deaf and hard of hearing students. The Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education. https://doi.org/10.1093/deafed/enac033
title: Use longitudinal data analysis to understand how DHH students' achievement progresses over time and where they need additional support
description: This principle holds that educators and researchers should use longitudinal data analysis to track how academic achievement for DHH students progresses over time. The article argues that "Longitudinal data analysis is critical to understanding how academic achievement for DHH students progresses over time and where they may need additional support on their academic journey to achieve at the level of their hearing peers." It grounds support decisions in multi-year growth evidence rather than single snapshots.
requirements: Longitudinal achievement data covering multiple grades and domains for DHH students
target_learners: Deaf and hard of hearing students
target_learning_goals: Identifying where DHH students need additional academic support
Achieving at the level of hearing peers
examples: The study analyzed MAP Growth data from grades 2 to 8 across seven reading and mathematics domains over 5 years to locate points where DHH students may need additional support

article_title: A longitudinal study of reading growth for students with visual impairments
citation: Boroson, Beth; Barker, Elizabeth; Li, Xueming (Sylvia). (2017). A longitudinal study of reading growth for students with visual impairments. Journal on Technology and Persons with Disabilities, 6, 158–171. https://www.nwea.org
title: Use longitudinal reading-growth data to set expectations for academic growth and inform instructional practices
description: The article argues that tracking students' reading development as they progress through school serves two purposes: it "provides expectations for academic growth and informs instructional practices." Applying this principle means analyzing longitudinal achievement data for a population of interest and using the resulting growth patterns to calibrate expectations and guide instruction, as the authors do for students with visual impairments.
requirements: Requires longitudinal achievement data covering students' progression through school grades
target_learners: Students with visual impairments in grades 3–10
target_learning_goals: Reading achievement and reading growth
examples: The authors analyzed eight years of MAP reading data for 224 students with visual impairments and compared their growth with a nationally normed general-population group

article_title: Portraits in Progress: Emerging Future-Ready Skills Assessment Strategies
citation: Kyle Dunbar, Katie Wilczak, Kelly Mills, Nick Mireles, and Alison Shell. (2025). Portraits in Progress: Emerging Future-Ready Skills Assessment Strategies. Digital Promise and Pearson. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Locally developed, grade-banded rubrics as the shared evaluation method across districts
description: Of the seven districts with assessments in place, all used locally developed, grade-banded rubrics to evaluate student evidence of Portrait of a Graduate skills. Rubrics identify outcomes and evidence representing specific performance levels, are typically developed at district level with educator input, and are accompanied by calibration sessions in which educators collectively score student work samples. Their strength is representing each district's unique context and goals; their challenge is potential wide variability in teachers' scores.
requirements: Calibration sessions where educators review and collectively score student work samples and unpack interpretations of rubric score levels
constraints: Locally-designed rubrics differ across districts, which limits comparability of scores across districts
target_learners: K-12 students assessed with district Portrait of a Graduate rubrics
target_learning_goals: future-ready skills and competencies defined in local Portrait frameworks
examples: Norwalk Public Schools teachers co-designed a critical thinking rubric using the district's learning progression

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work Beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities With Formative Assessment. WestEd, Region 15 Comprehensive Center. https://www.wested.org/
title: 1st/2nd grade poetry-analysis lesson with differentiated poem sets and scaffolded edge learning
description: An early elementary lesson example, inspired by a lesson taught by Olivia Lozano at the UCLA Lab School, in which 1st and 2nd grade English learners and monolingual peers analyze poetic devices such as rhyme and repeated line. Students receive "sets of poems of varying complexity," first work through a sample poem with the teacher, then analyze independently with teacher conferences and peer feedback. The brief notes scaffolding "supports students to work at the edge of their competencies" and that learning would not have been supported had the teacher analyzed the poem for the whole class.
requirements: Differentiated materials, independent analysis opportunities, evidence-based planning, and peer and teacher support structures
target_learners: 1st and 2nd grade English learners and monolingual English-speaking students
target_learning_goals: Identifying and describing grade-level poetic devices while developing language in context
examples: Students conference with the teacher and get feedback from peers during independent work time

article_title: Should Schools Be Conducting Lockdown Drills?
citation: Schildkraut, J., Grogan, K., & Nabors, A. (2020). Should schools be conducting lockdown drills? WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/schools-lockdown-drills/
title: Taxonomy distinguishing lockdown drills from active shooter drills and exercises
description: The brief argues that much confusion in the debate over school safety drills stems from muddling terminology. It defines "active shooter" as "one or more individuals actively engaged in killing or attempting to kill people in a populated area", whereas lockdowns are used for "any active threat inside a school or other location". It further distinguishes drills, performed by single entities to test a specific procedure, from exercises, which involve multiple agencies and test interagency cooperation. This taxonomy frames the article's argument that lockdown drills can be incorporated into the school day, whereas active shooter exercises require considerable planning and may be costly.
requirements: The distinction requires schools and districts to use consistent terminology when planning and mandating emergency drills.
constraints: The brief notes drills are often confused with exercises and with active shooter drills in public discussion, so the terms are "typically discussed as if they were one and the same".
target_learners: K-12 students
school faculty and staff
target_learning_goals: emergency preparedness
knowing how to respond during a lockdown
key_sources: Schildkraut, J., Grogan, K., & Nabors, A. (2020). Should schools be conducting lockdown drills? WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/schools-lockdown-drills/

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 1: The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, lead authors Aimee Evan, Laura Groth, and Hannah Sullivan. (2020). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Part 1 The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.org
title: Locally validate distress indicators before using them to flag struggling schools
description: The report cautions that charter contexts differ and early warning systems 'work best when locally validated.' The indicators it identifies 'should be the start to the conversation about what schools struggling in your jurisdiction look like, rather than the conclusion of the conversation,' ideally including stakeholders from varying levels of the charter sector working together to identify indicators.

constraints: Not all authorizers have the capacity or policy directives to collect and examine all potential indicators; authorizers must tailor actions to their state's legislation
target_learners: Charter school authorizers and state education agencies
target_learning_goals: Accurate early identification of schools in distress in a given jurisdiction
examples: The report's methodology section and 'Context is Everything' sidebar both direct readers to validate indicators against local historical patterns of school struggle

article_title: Standards-Based Education Reforms: Looking Back to Look Forward
citation: Kirst, M. W. (2024). Standards-based education reforms: Looking back to look forward. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/647.623
title: Loose coupling explains why standards policies disconnect from classroom outcomes
description: Loose coupling is the paper's central explanatory concept: educational organizations tend to disconnect policies from outcomes, so federal and state standards policies only weakly and inconsistently shape classroom teaching. The paper applies it system-wide, from Washington, DC to individual classrooms, arguing that classroom impact will be "highly inconsistent in the absence of thorough, targeted support on standards-aligned teaching methodologies or curriculum construction." It frames effective implementation as requiring buy-in at every level rather than top-down dictates.
requirements: Buy-in at the various levels of the system; policymakers cannot simply dictate from the top down
constraints: Classroom-level instructional impact is highly inconsistent absent thorough, targeted support on standards-aligned teaching or curriculum construction
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. public schools
target_learning_goals: Standards-aligned instruction in core academic content areas
key_sources: Kirst, M. W. (2024). Standards-based education reforms: Looking back to look forward. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/647.623

citation: Melnick, H., Wechsler, M. E., Wang, V., & Plasencia, S. (2026). Universal preschool in California: Promising practices for mixed delivery systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/724.211
title: Long Beach Early Learning Hub online enrollment system
description: The Long Beach Early Learning Hub is an online enrollment system developed collaboratively and hosted by the Mayor's Fund for Long Beach. According to the report, it "helps families find child care options and financial assistance." It is part of a broader city infrastructure that includes the Long Beach Early Childhood Education Committee, a partnership created in 2003 that unites district, city, nonprofit, and health partners around a shared strategic plan, and annual outreach events and a citywide conference for early educators across the mixed delivery system.

Hosting and maintenance by a coordinating organization (the Mayor's Fund for Long Beach)
target_learners: Families with children under age 5 in Long Beach
target_learning_goals: Family awareness of and equitable access to early learning programs
examples: The committee hosts annual festivals to help families learn about early learning programs and offers a citywide annual conference for early educators.

article_title: Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges
citation: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center
title: Loss and Momentum Framework for community college student progression
description: The loss and momentum framework organizes the community college experience into four stages of student progression — connection (interest to application), entry (enrollment to completion of gatekeeper courses), progress (entry into a course of study to 75 percent of requirements completed), and completion (complete course of study to credential with labor market value). For each stage it pairs common loss points, such as poor college counseling or part-time enrollment, with momentum strategies such as mandatory advising and accelerated programs. The guide states that "understanding when and why a college's students are slowed down or sidetracked in efforts to earn a credential is essential" for developing completion pathways, and the framework anchors the initiative's data-intensive Pathways Analysis.
requirements: A student data system spanning from day one to completion, plus student engagement and leadership focused on completion, frame the framework's use
constraints: Loss points and momentum strategies are presented as common impediments and responses, not as a validated causal model
target_learners: community college students, especially low-income students
target_learning_goals: timely attainment of credentials of value for further education and the labor market
examples: The framework diagram pairs loss points like delayed entry and limited advising with momentum strategies like dual enrollment, intrusive advising, and emergency aid
key_sources: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center

article_title: New Mexico Community School Profile: Los Padillas Elementary School
citation: Germain, E. (2024). New Mexico community school profile: Los Padillas Elementary School. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-school-los-padillas-brief
title: Los Padillas Wildlife Sanctuary (5-acre experiential education facility)
description: The Los Padillas Wildlife Sanctuary is a 5-acre experiential education facility on the school campus that was "in disrepair and out of use" in 2017 and revived at community insistence as an outdoor learning space. Fourth-graders completed a project-based pond-restoration unit, researching at ponds across town and learning from experts; Tribal leaders use the sanctuary's tree-stump seating area for storytelling about Native culture and history. APS helps maintain the grounds and arranges visits for every 3rd-grade class across the city.
requirements: Grounds maintenance support (APS works with the school to maintain the grounds)
Staffing including a naturalist teacher
constraints: Located far from many partners and resources in central Albuquerque
target_learners: Los Padillas students and every 3rd-grade class across Albuquerque Public Schools
target_learning_goals: Outdoor and nature education
Environmental science
Native culture and history
Project-based learning
examples: Fourth-graders learned to care for the overgrown pond, visiting ponds in town and learning from experts how to clean water and clear cattails responsibly.

article_title: Leveling the Playing Field: Temporal Video Segmentation for Individuals with ADHD in Computing Education
citation: Veronica Pimenova, Chris Lee, Baramee Bhakdibhumi, Simon Chu, and Andrew Begel. (2026). Leveling the Playing Field: Temporal Video Segmentation for Individuals with ADHD in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24612
title: Logic-aware segmented video intervention with fixed 4-second system-defined pauses
description: A post-hoc video processing intervention for instructional programming videos: after recording, content is cut at logical action boundaries and a fixed pause is injected after each step. The article explains that "a pause was manually inserted immediately after the completion of a logical action (e.g., snapping a block into place), but before the explanation of the subsequent step." Pausing is system-defined rather than student-initiated, chosen because student-initiated pausing often has negligible learning effects. Pause duration was set to 4 seconds after piloting 2-, 4-, and 6-second intervals with 13 participants.
requirements: Pre-recorded instructional videos whose content can be divided into discrete logical steps, with segment cuts agreed upon by multiple authors
constraints: The 4-second pause duration is fixed; the article acknowledges a one-size-fits-all pause duration may not be optimal for every learner
Evaluated with adult novices with no programming experience in the Scratch environment, which the authors note may limit generalizability
target_learners: adult novice programmers
individuals with ADHD in computing education
target_learning_goals: following instructional video steps to build a Scratch game
reducing errors and hesitations during programming tasks
examples: Six custom-made videos teaching a Cat and Mouse game in Scratch, segmented with Final Cut Pro, with pause durations matched audiovisually between conditions

article_title: Exploring student anxiety and experience in performance-based assessments using AIvaluate: an LLM-augmented emotionally
citation: Habeeb Yusuf, Arthur Money, Damon Daylamani-Zad. (2026). Exploring student anxiety and experience in performance-based assessments using AIvaluate: an LLM-augmented emotionally intelligent pedagogical AI conversational agent. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10634-x
title: Logic model of how technology mediation may reduce anxiety in viva voce performance-based assessments
description: The article proposes a logic model structuring how technology may reduce anxiety in viva voce assessments, organised as Inputs (technology mediation, assessment context, learner factors), Theoretical Mechanisms (social evaluation theory, cognitive load, the affective filter hypothesis, the Technology Acceptance Model, psychological safety), Mediators (reduced perceived social threat, increased autonomy and pacing control), and Outcomes. The article states that "Inputs refer to the contextual and design factors that shape the assessment environment" and that outcomes include "state anxiety reduced", improved self-regulation, reduced extraneous load and increased cognitive availability, culminating in enhanced demonstration of competence.
requirements: Technology-mediated assessment environments that reduce direct exposure to authority figures and allow students to pace, pause or reflect before responding
constraints: The model is a theoretical structure proposed by the authors; the study measured emotional and usability outcomes but did not record formal performance scores
target_learners: learners undertaking oral performance-based assessments, particularly those with social anxiety or neurodivergence
target_learning_goals: valid demonstration of competence in oral assessment through reduced anxiety and increased cognitive availability
examples: The model underpins AIvaluate, whose pacing, mediated interaction and emotional-state-aware suggested replies instantiate the inputs and mediators the model describes

article_title: DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation
citation: Vishal Kumar, Shubhra Mishra, Rebecca Hao, Rizwaan Malik, David Broman, Dorottya Demszky. (2025). DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation. NeurIPS 2025 Workshop: MATH-AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08283
title: Build education-technology evaluation on lightweight, low-cost pipelines that work with smaller models
description: The article argues that equitable education technology requires evaluation methods that run reliably and cheaply at scale, rather than depending on expensive frontier models. It states that "For education technology to be truly equitable, evaluation methods must work reliably with open models and lightweight pipelines that can be deployed at scale at low costs", and that AI education tools "need to be built at the lowest cost possible". Task-specific automated pipelines combining symbolic abstraction with lightweight inference are its proposed route.
requirements: Decoupling perception from verification so that validators can run without a large model
constraints: Closed-source frontier models are costly and impractical for resource-constrained educational deployments, per the article
target_learners: K-12 mathematics educators and their students in resource-constrained settings
target_learning_goals: Reliable automated quality evaluation of AI-generated instructional diagrams
examples: DiagramIR enabled GPT-4.1-Mini to evaluate diagrams comparably to GPT-5 as a judge at 10.3x lower total dataset cost

article_title: From Heuristics to Analytics: Forecasting Effort and Progress in Online Learning
citation: Eric S. Qiu, Danielle R. Thomas, Boyuan Guo, Vincent Aleven, Conrad Borchers. (2026). From Heuristics to Analytics: Forecasting Effort and Progress in Online Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12788
title: Longitudinal middle-school ITS log dataset with weekly engagement targets
description: A longitudinal dataset of web-based ITS usage for middle-school mathematics. The article states: "The dataset comprises activity logs collected from 425 students over 39 weeks (October 2010 to May 2012), capturing 2.9 million student-problem interactions." It yields 11,710 student-week observations and supports two weekly targets built by aggregating ISO-week minutes and counting new AFM-mastered skills, with outliers removed via Tukey's Fence (k=1.5). It underpins all benchmarking, feature-importance, and ablation analyses in the paper.
requirements: Event-level logs with timestamps, durations, learning outcomes, knowledge components, opportunity counts, and problem identifiers, compatible with DataShop log standards
constraints: Drawn from a single ITS and subject domain in 2010-2012; some inputs such as opportunity counters and skill tags are not universal across platforms
target_learners: middle-school mathematics students using ITS
target_learning_goals: weekly practice effort and skill mastery tracking
examples: 425 students, 39 weeks, 2.9 million interactions; students averaged 39.8±14.7 minutes per week
key_sources: Eric S. Qiu, Danielle R. Thomas, Boyuan Guo, Vincent Aleven, Conrad Borchers. (2026). From Heuristics to Analytics: Forecasting Effort and Progress in Online Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12788

article_title: ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education
citation: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662
title: Deploy educational GenAI locally first so student data stays within the institutional boundary
description: The article argues that GenAI tutoring in schools should follow a local-first principle: inference runs on institutional hardware rather than cloud services. The authors state the pipeline "can run without external cloud dependencies, which (i) reduces recurring costs, (ii) enables offline operation, and (iii) strengthens privacy-by-design by keeping student interactions within the institutional boundary". This addresses data-sovereignty and compliance concerns that make cloud LLM services difficult for schools to adopt at scale.
requirements: Local or on-premise compute capable of hosting the LLM and TTS models
Institutional governance over configuration and knowledge sources
constraints: Particularly relevant for European educational contexts where data protection constraints and procurement limitations hinder cloud adoption; under-resourced institutions may lack suitable local hardware
target_learners: students in public schools, including under-resourced and rural contexts
target_learning_goals: privacy-preserving, institutionally governed AI-supported tutoring
examples: The prototype's server-side pipeline ran entirely locally without reliance on cloud infrastructure, with speech recognition performed on-device and TTS executed on a local machine
key_sources: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662

article_title: Automated Grading of Handwritten Mathematics Using Vision-Capable LLMs
citation: Jacob Levine, Miguel Aenlle, Craig Zilles, Matthew West, and Mariana Silva. (2026). Automated Grading of Handwritten Mathematics Using Vision-Capable LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19043
title: Deploy vision-LLM handwritten-math grading in low-stakes formative contexts first, with students informed feedback may contain mistakes
description: The article concludes that Gemini 3 Flash's accuracy appears sufficient for low-stakes, formative contexts such as practice problems, where immediate feedback outweighs occasional errors, provided students are informed the AI-generated feedback may contain mistakes. High-stakes deployment demands greater reliability in interpreting student work. This principle scopes deployment recommendations to the accuracy levels the study measured.
requirements: Students are informed the AI-generated feedback may contain mistakes
Accuracy sufficient for the stakes level, as measured against human ground truth
constraints: High-stakes deployment demands greater reliability in interpreting student work
target_learners: university STEM students in practice and formative assessment contexts
target_learning_goals: immediate feedback on handwritten mathematical problem solving
examples: The study evaluated the grader on extra-credit in-lecture activities and proctored midterm submissions, with students never exposed to AI-generated grading output

article_title: A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community
citation: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community.
title: Workshop session structure: local data, small-group testing, collective discussion
description: Each of the six sessions followed a common three-part structure: facilitators presented local data or department-sourced materials, faculty tested and reflected on the materials in small groups, and the whole group discussed them together. The article states: "We started by sharing local data, whether around AI policies and use or activities gathered from different courses, and then had faculty test and reflect on the materials in small groups, followed by collective discussion." This structure embodies the framework's principles of leading with student use and facilitating collective inquiry rather than disseminating best practices.
requirements: Local data and department-sourced materials must be available to anchor each session
constraints: Framed as collective, local inquiry rather than a general faculty training workshop
target_learners: University physics faculty in a departmental learning community
target_learning_goals: Developing shared departmental approaches to AI use in courses
examples: Session 3 opened with survey data on students' correctness-checking, then faculty tested AI chatbots on real anonymized homework in small groups before collective discussion

article_title: 'Problem-Based Learning and the Structural Conditions for Productive AI Integration'
citation: Michael Rowe. (2026). Problem-based learning and the structural conditions for productive AI integration. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/haet3_v1
title: Load-bearing versus offloadable cognitive demand determines whether AI offloading is formative
description: The essay reframes the cognitive offloading concern: the question is not whether AI removes cognitive demand but whether the removed demand was building a capability the learner needs. Load-bearing demand (judgement, reasoning, professional identity) cannot be offloaded without developmental loss; offloadable demand (retrieval, formatting, production mechanics) can be. The essay states: "Not all cognitive demand is equally formative." It grounds the distinction in Rowe and Lynch's (2025) information context / personal context framework around context sovereignty.
requirements: A diagnostic account of which layer of difficulty each cognitive task builds, distinguishing writing-as-thinking from writing-as-production
constraints: What counts as relevant judgement is culturally situated and varies across healthcare systems and professional traditions; the universality claim is about the layer, not what fills it
target_learners: health professions students in higher education
target_learning_goals: professional judgement
distinguishing formative from offloadable cognitive work
examples: A nursing student may offload database searching and summarisation without developmental cost, but not the judgement about whether evidence applies to a specific patient and ward

article_title: Obtaining more out of less text in CBI: effects of varied text density levels as a function of learner characteristics and control strategy
citation: Ross, S. M., Morrison, G. R., & O'Dell, J. K. (1988). Obtaining More out of Less Text in CBI: Effects of Varied Text Density Levels as a Function of Learner Characteristics and Control Strategy. Educational Communication and Technology, 36(3), 131-142. http://www.jstor.org/stable/30218252
title: Offer low-density text as a standard feature or learner-control option in expository CBI lessons
description: This principle holds that CBI lessons presenting expository material should limit on-screen text to essential words and phrases, since low-density presentations reduced lesson length and reading time without harming learning of facts and concepts. The article recommends that "The availability of low-density text as a standard feature or learner-control option in expository lessons deserves further consideration as a design alternative." It may also make difficult material appear less threatening and easier to read.
requirements: Content must remain unchanged when density is reduced; only modifiers, articles, and non-essential sentences are deleted, keeping the basic information and support material the same.
constraints: The article notes elaborated text should not be discouraged generally, since it is advantageous for learning complex procedural skills and for developing reading and writing skills; low-density use is suggested where displaying long text segments is difficult or costly, as in CBI.
target_learners: undergraduate teacher education majors learning expository statistics content
target_learning_goals: recall of facts and conceptual information, such as central tendency measures
examples: The study developed low-density versions of a five-lesson statistics unit by rules such as reducing sentences to main ideas, using outline form, and deleting non-informative sentences, yielding a 56% word savings with equal achievement.

article_title: Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish‐learning children
citation: Hurtado Nereyda, Marchman Virginia A., Fernald Anne. (2008). Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish-learning children. Developmental Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2898277/
title: Looking-while-listening eye-tracking procedure for measuring infants' real-time speech processing efficiency
description: The looking-while-listening procedure assesses efficiency of online spoken language comprehension in infants and toddlers. On each trial children see pictures of two familiar objects and hear speech naming one; gaze patterns are videotaped and coded frame-by-frame, yielding a high-resolution record of eye movements aligned with target noun onset, with inter-observer agreement averaging 97%. In this study it yielded mean reaction times for shifting from distracter to target picture at 18 and 24 months, used as the measure of speech processing efficiency.
requirements: Familiar target nouns known to most children at the testing age
Trials where the child starts on the distracter and shifts to the target within 300–1800 ms of target-word onset
Frame-by-frame coding of gaze patterns by trained observers
constraints: Mean RTs are based on different numbers of trials across participants because children vary in the likelihood they start on the distracter by chance
target_learners: Infants and toddlers aged 18 to 24 months learning Spanish as a first language
target_learning_goals: Measuring efficiency of real-time spoken word recognition and comprehension
examples: Eight target nouns at 18 months (32 test trials) and four more added at 24 months (36 test trials), stimuli controlled for prosodic comparability, target pictures matched for visual salience and grammatical gender

article_title: What Connections Can We Draw Between Research on Long‐Term Memory and Student Learning?
citation: Fandakova, Yana; Bunge, Silvia A. (2016). What Connections Can We Draw Between Research on Long-Term Memory and Student Learning? Mind, Brain and Education, 10(3). https://doi.org/10.1111/mbe.12123
title: Taxonomy of long-term memory systems relevant to classroom learning
description: The article presents a taxonomy of long-term memory as a framework for educators: long-term memory refers to "memory traces that last for days, months, or years" and is comprised of different systems associated with distinct biological substrates, including episodic memory for events rich in contextual detail, semantic memory for context-independent facts and concepts, and procedural skills. It explains that episodic memory relies heavily on the hippocampus whereas semantic memory depends on distributed cortical representations, and that these systems interact during learning.
requirements: Distinguishing memory forms by their content (events vs. facts vs. skills) and neural substrates
constraints: The article focuses on the forms of long-term memory most directly relevant to classroom learning, not all forms
target_learners: school-age children and adolescents
target_learning_goals: understanding how memory systems support academic learning such as reading, language comprehension, and arithmetic
examples: The article contrasts remembering seeing a lion at the zoo (episodic) with knowing that male lions have manes (semantic)

article_title: Bridging domains: examining the effects of relevance instructions and guiding questions on pre-service teachers’ first- and second-order knowledge integration
citation: Lehmann, T. (2024). Bridging domains: examining the effects of relevance instructions and guiding questions on pre-service teachers' first- and second-order knowledge integration. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09655-3
title: Use low-threshold instructional prompts — relevance instructions and guiding questions — to foster knowledge integration when pre-service teachers read and write across domain-specific texts
description: Because curricular integration of CK-, PK-, and PCK-specific courses is organizationally costly, the article promotes "rather easy-to-implement instructional scaffolds such as prompts to promote pre-service teachers' knowledge integration within self-regulated learning scenarios" involving multiple domain-specific texts and writing to learn. merging CK, PK, and PCK into an integrated knowledge base
examples: The GQ group received five guiding questions such as "Can you find statements in a text that can be used to explain the content that is presented in the other texts?"; the RI group received a text explaining why integrating CK, PK, and PCK matters, linked to the upcoming writing task

This principle recommends deploying paraprofessionals, pedagogues, or parent volunteers in in-class supporting roles as a cost-effective alternative to fully qualified co-teachers for raising achievement.

article_title: The Evolution of “Loaded Moments” Toward Escalation or De-Escalation in Student–Teacher Interactions
citation: Kennedy, B L & Junker, R (2024). The Evolution of “Loaded Moments” Toward Escalation or De-Escalation in Student–Teacher Interactions. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231202509
title: Loaded moments framework for the co-construction of escalation and de-escalation in student–teacher interactions
description: The review defines loaded moments as “points in time when two or more parties realize that their needs differ and that they must confront that difference.” It synthesizes 30 studies (2000–2020) into a staged process account: macro contexts set the scene, instigating circumstances co-construct incompatibilities, moment-by-moment co-construction drives (de)escalation, and outcomes feed long-term relationship and bond development. The framework organizes classroom conflict research around co-construction rather than individual blame.
requirements: Studies must describe the evolution of loaded moments between teachers and students during classroom interactions
constraints: Synthesis limited to 30 studies published from 2000 to 2020
target_learners: K-12 and school students in classroom settings
target_learning_goals: Successful negotiation of loaded moments to minimize negative interactions and their impacts

article_title: Practice Recommendations or Not? The LoGeT Model as Empirical Approach to Generate Localized, Generalized, and Transferable Evidence
citation: Lachner, A., Sibley, L., & Wagner, S. (2024). Practice Recommendations or Not? The LoGeT Model as Empirical Approach to Generate Localized, Generalized, and Transferable Evidence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09876-z
title: The LoGeT model: a three-stage, reciprocal framework integrating co-design, ManyClasses, and transfer strategies
description: The LoGeT model is a methodological framework for generating educational evidence that is localized, generalizable, and transferable. The authors state: "we propose the localize, generalize, and transfer (LoGeT) model to localize, generalize, and transfer scientific evidence for educational practice." It comprises a localization stage (co-design of interventions with teachers via context inquiry, participatory design, product design, and prototype-as-hypothesis phases), a generalization stage (implementing the interventions across diverse subjects, cohorts, and contexts and aggregating results with meta-analytic techniques such as mixed effect models), and a transfer stage (publishing materials as OER and communicating findings through practice-oriented outlets). The model is explicitly reciprocal rather than sequential, so transfer insights feed back into localization and generalization.
requirements: Interdisciplinary design teams including several subject-matter teachers and researchers simultaneously, so abstract design principles are localized in authentic subject-specific teaching experiences
A joint design framework and iterative formative feedback workshops to warrant comparability and implementation fidelity across localized realizations
constraints: Contextual findings from the generalization stage cannot be interpreted as causal, but rather inform future experimental studies
Findings may be confounded by teacher motivation and implementation fidelity because participation depends on motivated teachers
The procedure requires considerable research efforts, infrastructure, funding for teachers, and professionals for science communication
target_learners: Educational researchers
Teachers and teacher educators
Pre-service teachers
School students across subjects and school types
target_learning_goals: Effectiveness of instructional interventions across instructional contexts
Evidence-based design and transfer of educational interventions
examples: Three long-term projects applied the model: a TPACK teacher-education project with five design teams, a 4-year adaptive-teaching project at comprehensive schools, and a minimal-invasive non-interactive teaching project in a master's program.

article_title: Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology
citation: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w
title: Load Reduction Instruction: five sequenced principles from difficulty reduction to guided independent learning
description: Load Reduction Instruction (LRI) is an integrative instructional framework drawing on Cognitive Load Theory that harmonizes explicit instruction with guided independent learning. Its first four principles build long-term memory and fluency: "Reduce the difficulty of instruction in the initial stages of learning", provide support and scaffolding, allow sufficient opportunity for practice, and provide feedback-feedforward. The fifth principle, guided independent learning, is introduced once fluency and automaticity develop, and "represents a fundamental unification of explicit and constructivist instructional approaches." Teaching strategies operationalizing each principle are mapped in Tables 1 through 5.
requirements: Sequencing is pivotal: explicit principles #1-4 precede guided independence (#5), calibrated to the learner's prior knowledge and novice-to-expert status
constraints: LRI targets reduction of extraneous cognitive load as the main yield and intrinsic load as a subsidiary yield; failure to reduce load for novices risks a failure to learn
target_learners: school students moving from novice to more expert status
target_learning_goals: managing cognitive load to optimize learning and enable guided independent learning
examples: Table 1 strategies for difficulty reduction include pre-training, modelling, segmenting, and preliminary and spaced reviews; Table 2 includes worked examples, templates, prompting, and personalizing

article_title: How Many Classes and Students Should Ideally be Sampled When Assessing the Role of Classroom Climate via Student Ratings on a Limited Budget? An Optimal Design Perspective
citation: Steffen Zitzmann, Wolfgang Wagner, Martin Hecht, Christoph Helm, Christian Fischer, Lisa Bardach, Richard Göllner. (2021). How Many Classes and Students Should Ideally be Sampled When Assessing the Role of Classroom Climate via Student Ratings on a Limited Budget? An Optimal Design Perspective. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:511–536. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09635-4
title: Treat optimal designs as locally optimal and apply a rule of thumb when the optimal number of students per class exceeds typical class size
description: The article cautions that "the optimal design is only 'locally optimal,' meaning that it is optimal only for the specific values that the researcher specified for the quantities and can be suboptimal for other values," suggesting maximin designs as a workaround. It also notes that power computations assume unbiased estimation, which holds in large samples but not small ones, and offers a practical rule: "set this number to 25 and then increase the number of classes to compensate for the loss of power" when the optimal students per class exceeds typical class size.
requirements: Planners must specify plausible values for the ICC(1)s and slopes, ideally drawn from previous studies, and consider boundary conditions such as typical class size
constraints: Optimal designs can deviate from what is really optimal when assumed values are wrong or when sample sizes are small (results tend to be biased when sample sizes are small, e.g., below N > 1,000)
target_learners: Educational researchers planning classroom climate studies
Grant writers designing studies
target_learning_goals: Designing sufficiently powered, cost-efficient classroom climate studies
examples: The article suggests maximin designs, which maximize the minimum variability across a range of reasonable values for the quantities, as one workaround for the local optimality problem

citation: Evans, P., Vansteenkiste, M., Parker, P., Kingsford-Smith, A., & Zhou, S. (2024). Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09841-2
title: Load Reduction Instruction (LRI) framework of five instructional principles
description: Load reduction instruction integrates cognitive load theory findings into "a framework of instructional principles hypothesized to reduce cognitive load: reduce difficulty, provide support and scaffolding, create opportunities for practice, give useful feedback, and design guided, independent projects when learners have sufficient prior knowledge to experience success." It is measured by the 25-item LRIS as a higher-order factor with five principle subscales, validated with high school students and positively associated with motivation and achievement across school subjects.

constraints: Guided independent projects are recommended only when learners have sufficient prior knowledge to experience success

article_title: Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning
citation: Sibley, L., Fabian, A., Plicht, C., Pagano, L., Ehrhardt, N., Wellert, L., Bohl, T., & Lachner, A. (2025). Adaptive teaching with technology enhances lasting learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102141
title: LoGeT framework: Localize-Generalize-Transfer for scaling educational interventions
description: The Localize-Generalize-Transfer (LoGeT) framework by Lachner et al. structures implementation research so evidence is grounded in real classrooms yet generalizable. "The LoGeT model integrates three essential stages: localization, generalization, and transfer." Localization uses co-design with teachers as key stakeholders; generalization applies the ManyClasses approach, running the same experimental setup across multiple settings, subjects, and student groups; transfer creates practical resources such as instructional guides so educators can implement the strategies beyond the original study. This study instantiated LoGeT by combining co-design with a ManyClasses design across 12 units.
requirements: Research team participation in co-design support meetings to ensure implementation fidelity
constraints: ManyClasses units are intentionally diverse and not directly comparable in difficulty across subjects

citation: Lowell, Frances. (1917). A Preliminary Report of Some Group Tests of General Intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Design criteria for group intelligence tests in the primary grades
description: Lowell sets out a framework of requirements a test must meet to be administered to a group of young children rather than individually. She states that "Simplicity is an important criterion in the selection of the group test; simplicity of material; of directions; of response; and of scoring." Tests must permit only one correct response with one interpretation, be scored "all or none" so the examiner's judgment never enters, and directions must be clear, brief and repetitively illustrated since young children are limited in vocabulary and attention.
requirements: Material must be easily carried and quickly distributed to a large group, which the author achieved by arranging all pages and blanks in numbered booklets
constraints: Directions cannot be too varied, because too many instructions may destroy the value of the test, since ability to follow directions is itself a test of intelligence
target_learners: Children in first, second and third grades of elementary school
target_learning_goals: Screening for general intelligence level to identify children needing individual Binet testing
examples: The battery of twenty-five tests arranged as five-, six-, seven-, eight- and nine-year tests, adapted from Binet-Simon, Kuhlmann's 1917 Revision, Terman's Revision, the New York Bureau standards, and original tests

article_title: Which class matters? Juxtaposing multiple class environments as frames-of-reference for academic self-concept formation.
citation: Fleischmann, M., Hübner, N., Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Trautwein, U., & Nagengast, B. (2021). Which Class Matters? Juxtaposing Multiple Class Environments as Frames-of-Reference for Academic Self-Concept Formation.

description: The frame-of-reference account holds that academic self-concept is formed through social comparison with the achievement of surrounding educational environments, producing the big-fish-little-pond effect (BFLPE). The local dominance effect specifies that the most locally proximal comparison group matters most: prior three-level work "found the class to be the pivotal frame-of-reference for academic self-concept formation," and local comparison information "matters the most for ability self-evaluations." This study extends the account to course-by-course tracked systems with multiple class environments.
requirements: Data must allow reliable achievement aggregates at every level of student nesting, which large-scale datasets like PISA and TIMSS typically do not provide
constraints: The article notes average achievement of educational environments is highly correlated, making the relative strength of frames-of-reference difficult to identify
target_learners: eighth-grade students in course-by-course tracked secondary school systems
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept in mathematics
examples: The study regressed math self-concept on average math achievement of students' school, math class, and regular class simultaneously in cross-classified multilevel models.

article_title: Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence.
citation: De Sanctis, S. (1911). Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 498-507.
title: Two-tier theory of ideation: lower associative processes and higher ideation, with intelligence as elaboration of the lower
description: De Sanctis divides mental processes into immediate ones governed by the laws of association (sense perception, imagination, memory) and mediate or higher processes (judgment, concept formation, reasoning). He holds that "Intelligence, properly so called, or intellectual capacity, is a manifestation of higher ideation," while insisting there is "no discontinuity between them, but rather a progressive evolution." requirements: Measurement of intelligence must be interpreted as measurement of the level of higher ideation, not of elementary sensations, attention or memory alone
constraints: The author warns against positing new metaphysical entities, which he calls superfluous and even dangerous for experimental psychology

mental defectives

target_learning_goals: understanding the structure of intellectual capacity as a basis for its measurement

article_title: A methodological perspective on learning in the developing brain
citation: van Duijvenvoorde, A. C. K., Whitmore, L. B., Westhoff, B. & Mills, K. L. (2022). A methodological perspective on learning in the developing brain. npj Science of Learning 7:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00127-w

description: The review recommends repeatedly measuring the same individuals over time, ideally with an intervention and matched comparison, when studying learning in a brain that is simultaneously maturing. article_title: Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times
citation: Pelánek, R., & Jarušek, P. (2015). Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0048-x
title: Log-linear model of problem solving times analogical to the IRT three-parameter model
description: A generative student model for interactive problem solving that specifies the distribution of problem solving times rather than correctness probability. It assumes, in the article's words, "a linear relationship between a problem solving skill and a logarithm of time to solve a problem": tsp = bp + apθs + N(0, cp²), where b is basic difficulty, a a discrimination factor, and c a randomness factor. The notation is deliberately chosen to mirror the IRT three-parameter logistic model, and the model is also related to k=1 collaborative filtering. requirements: Times are log-transformed and only successfully completed problems are modeled; normalization sets mean skill 0 and mean discrimination -1 to resolve scale indeterminacy
constraints: Applicable to well-structured problems where the solution cannot be guessed and solving time is a sufficient performance measure
target_learners: university and high school students practicing programming, mathematics, and logic puzzles
target_learning_goals: problem solving skill estimation and problem difficulty calibration in adaptive practice
examples: Used in the Problem Solving Tutor to predict solving times and recommend problems of suitable difficulty

Because the study found grades plateau at five or more active days per week, the authors propose that "setting lower physical activity targets such as accruing at least 60 min of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity on five out of seven days of the week could address the knowledge translation issue of an all-or-nothing threshold-based approach" and give adolescents actionable guidance for improving their grades.
requirements: Targets must be framed as attainable sub-guideline amounts rather than all-or-nothing thresholds, so students perceive they can act on them.
constraints: Based on self-reported grades and activity from a cross-sectional survey; the activity measure did not capture light-intensity activity, which may also benefit academic achievement.
target_learners: Adolescents in grades 9–12
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement (self-reported school grades)
examples: The study's spline models showed relatively linear grade improvements between one and five days of weekly activity, with a plateau at five or more days.
key_sources: Brown Denver M. Y., Porter Carah, Hamilton Faith, Almanza Fernanda, Narvid Christina, Pish Megan, Arizabalo Diego. (2022). Interactive Associations between Physical Activity and Sleep Duration in Relation to Adolescent Academic Achievement. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192315604

article_title: Low-tech intraocular ophthalmic microsurgery simulation: A low-cost model for home use.
citation: Golash Vidushi, Kaur Simerdip, Naveed Hasan, Nanavaty Mayank A. (2021). Low-tech intraocular ophthalmic microsurgery simulation: A low-cost model for home use. Indian Journal of Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.4103/ijo.IJO_242_21
title: Use low-cost home simulation as a regular adjunct to surgical training when facility access is limited
description: When trainees cannot access simulation facilities because of cost, location, or disrupted clinical training, the article recommends regular home-based simulation with a smartphone and household materials as an adjunct to patient-facing surgical training. It argues the model "provides an easy, portable, and reproducible method of simulation" and that enabling practice at home or at the workplace "does not require any additional expense, thereby minimizing cost and resource barriers".
requirements: Trainees need access to a smartphone they already own and basic disposable surgical instruments as described in the technique
constraints: The article states the model is a low-fidelity adjunct and "cannot replace simulation training models using microscopes, vegetables, and animal tissue with real instruments in a theater setting"
target_learners: ophthalmology surgical trainees
trainees without access to simulation facilities
target_learning_goals: maintenance of manual dexterity and surgical skills
basic intraocular surgical technique
examples: The authors propose regular use of the model "as an adjunct to surgical training" in a context of social distancing and limited financial resources

title: Facilities with very low incidence of cardiac arrest should not be exempted from implementing a rapid response system with standardised protocols and annual drills
description: The article recommends that "Facilities with very low incidences of sudden patient deterioration and cardiac arrest should not be excepted from implementing an RRS, standardising the protocol for resuscitation and annual drills to train and monitor the knowledge and skills of the front-line staff." The absence of previous cardiac arrest at GHMC had led to low awareness and preparedness among staff, so continuous training is needed to sustain awareness given high staff turnover and the rarity of serious cases.

awareness and preparedness for rare critical events

article_title: Latent Safety Threats and Countermeasures in the Operating Theater: A National In Situ Simulation-Based Observational Study.
citation: Long Jennifer A., Webster Craig S., Holliday Timothy, Torrie Jane, Weller Jennifer M. (2022). Latent Safety Threats and Countermeasures in the Operating Theater: A National In Situ Simulation-Based Observational Study. Simulation in Healthcare 17(1). https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000547
title: London Protocol contributory factors framework for categorizing latent safety threats
description: The London Protocol contributory factors framework is a comprehensive taxonomy of system threats ranging from proximal to distal, used in this study to code latent safety threats identified during in situ simulation. The article explains that "The set of 'contributory factors' in the London Protocol range from proximal threats such as staff skillsets and patient characteristics to more distal threats such as management decisions and organizational processes." The framework spans seven factor types (patient, task and technology, individual staff, team, work environment, organizational and management, institutional context), and the authors added three subcategories (task distribution, knowing names of team members, medication storage) where existing subcategories did not describe observed threats.
requirements: A data dictionary with a specific definition of each LST subcategory to support consistent coding
Coders conferring across clinical and nonclinical backgrounds until coding consistently
constraints: Some LSTs did not map onto existing subcategories, requiring three additional subcategories developed by the authors
target_learners: Multidisciplinary operating theater teams (anesthetists, surgeons, technicians, theater nurses)
target_learning_goals: Identifying and categorizing system-level threats to patient safety in clinical environments
examples: The study coded 77 postcourse reports into the framework's subcategories, with interrater reliability κ = 0.78 in a sample of 10 independently coded events

article_title: Teacher Evaluation of an Experiential Vegetable Education Program for Australian Primary Schools: Does Face-to-Face Training Add Value above Digital Training?
citation: Poelman A. A. M., Cochet-Broch M., Beelen J., Wiggins B., Heffernan J. E., & Cox D. N. (2021). Teacher Evaluation of an Experiential Vegetable Education Program for Australian Primary Schools: Does Face-to-Face Training Add Value above Digital Training? Nutrients, 13(5), 1648. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu13051648
title: LORI-based teacher acceptability survey instrument for digital training and classroom programs
description: The study used an online survey rating agreement with statements on 5-point Likert scales: 15 statements for the online training module (14 based on the Learning Object Review Instrument, LORI) and 18 statements for the program covering 8 of 9 LORI dimensions plus feasibility. Eleven statements were identical to those used in a prior evaluation, enabling direct comparison across program versions.
requirements: Constructs require sufficient internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha > 0.70) for averaging; where lower (e.g., interaction usability α = 0.69; feasibility α = 0.68), items are analysed separately with medians due to skewed distributions
constraints: Some LORI dimensions were deemed not applicable (feedback and adaptation) or not relevant (accessibility and standard compliance) to the online module
target_learners: Primary school teachers implementing an education program
target_learning_goals: Evaluate acceptability, feasibility and reusability of teacher training and classroom program resources
examples: The feasibility construct was added because it was deemed important for teacher uptake, and an overall program score out of 10 plus open-ended questions on best features and improvements were included.

article_title: Development and validation of a simulator for teaching minimally invasive thoracic surgery in Brazil.
citation: Martins Francisco Neto et al. (2021). Development and validation of a simulator for teaching minimally invasive thoracic surgery in Brazil. Acta Cirúrgica Brasileira. https://doi.org/10.1590/ACB360508
title: Use low-cost physical simulators for VATS training where virtual simulators and live-animal models are unaffordable
description: The article recommends simulation-based training outside the operating room because it offers unlimited repetitions without harming patients, and argues that in contexts like Brazil, where virtual simulators are costly and few models exist, a locally built physical console is a practical alternative. It notes the simulator "can be transported and used anywhere, at an affordable cost". The principle is grounded in the simulator's validation results.
requirements: A realistic reproduction of the target anatomy and port triangulation, validated for face, content and construct validity
constraints: No translational validation of operating-room performance transfer was performed
target_learners: thoracic surgery residents
thoracic surgeons learning VATS
target_learning_goals: endoscopic suturing and three-port VATS technical skills
examples: The fiberglass console with TPE lung was built for about US$ 1,200 and used for a three-stage pulmonary suture experiment at a national congress

article_title: The use of the online Inverted Classroom Model for digital teaching with gamification in medical studies.
citation: Huber J, Witti M, Schunk M, Fischer MR, Tolks D. (2021). The use of the online Inverted Classroom Model for digital teaching with gamification in medical studies. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2021-38/zma001399.shtml
title: Online ICM version of the seminar 'The Lonely Patient' with synchronous Zoom sessions and Kahoot!
description: A case-based seminar on the German health care system, taught from a patient's perspective, redesigned as a purely digital online Inverted Classroom course during COVID-19. Students acquire factual knowledge in a self-study phase with instructional videos, then join a synchronous, interactive, learner-centered Zoom session where "The gamified Audience Response System (ARS) Kahoot! was used to activate students", an online quiz system with points, badges and leaderboards. The existing online self-learning phase could be reused directly, so adjustments concerned only the former classroom part.
requirements: An existing ICM self-study phase with digital learning materials that can be reused directly
A video conference system for synchronous teaching and a gamified audience response system for activation
constraints: Developed quickly under emergency remote teaching conditions during the COVID-19 pandemic
target_learners: medical students in health systems, health economics and public health care (GGG)
target_learning_goals: understanding the German health care system from the patient's perspective
factual knowledge acquisition via defined learning goals
interaction and discussion of the patient case
examples: In the winter semester of 2018/19 a 15-minute ICM-based online self-learning phase was developed; existing written materials (patient case, factsheets) were transformed into two to three minute instructional videos.

article_title: A Cocurricular Program That Encourages Specific Study Skills and Habits Improves Academic Performance and Retention of First-Year Undergraduates in Introductory Biology.
citation: Hawkins Whitney, W.; Goddard, K.; Favero, C. (2021). A Cocurricular Program That Encourages Specific Study Skills and Habits Improves Academic Performance and Retention of First-Year Undergraduates in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.20-06-0117
title: Logistic regression preparedness model predicting probability of achieving a C+ or better in Bio101
description: A logistic regression model trained on 2013–2016 cohort data (n = 638) using sex, first-generation status, Pell eligibility, underrepresented minority status, athlete status, high school calculus grade, unweighted core high school GPA, and SAT score to predict each student's probability of achieving a C+ or better. The article reports that "For the 2017 cohort, the model correctly classified students in 84% of cases." Students were then banded into low (≤25%), medium (26–84%), and high (≥85%) preparedness groups to target recruitment and compare outcomes.
requirements: Multiple years of prior cohort data with demographic and academic variables to train the model
Concordance tables to convert ACT scores and post-2016 SAT scores; a second model omitting testing for students without scores
constraints: The authors recommend institutions "consider which variables might be applicable on their own campuses and build a model that best predicts the performance of their own students"
Neither SAT nor ACT scores were available for a small percentage of test-optional students
target_learners: First-year, first-time undergraduates entering a STEM gateway course
target_learning_goals: Early identification of students likely to struggle so support can be offered before failure
examples: In 2018 the model was used to recruit students with a probability of 60% or lower of achieving a C+ or better

citation: Favier V., Kimmoun A., Gatin A., Gallet P. (2020). Percutaneous tracheostomy simulation training for ENT physicians in the treatment of COVID-19-positive patients. European Annals of Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Diseases. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anorl.2020.06.002
title: Low-tech procedural simulator built from anaesthesia circuit tubing for pre-training tracheostomy steps
description: A homemade simulator costing less than €20, made from an annealed anaesthesia ventilation circuit tube simulating the thyroid cartilage and glottis, an electric sheath for the cricoid, a foam or silicone support, and non-woven adhesive bands coated in liquid silicone as incisable skin. The authors write: "The second phase involves a homemade low-tech procedure simulator, costing less than €20 (Fig. 2), for practice ahead of full-scale simulation." It lets trainees practise kit handling and procedure steps before full-scale simulation.
requirements: Supervised use, so trainees practise the various parts of the kit and the successive steps before full-scale scenarios
constraints: It addresses the purely technical aspect of the training, not full-scale clinical decision-making
target_learners: ENT physicians in training for percutaneous tracheostomy
target_learning_goals: Master the manual steps of percutaneous tracheostomy and identify technical issues before full-scale simulation
examples: The authors state the low-tech simulator "provided prior identification of technical issues liable to slow down the procedure, and enhanced its safety"

citation: Fonseca LMM, Monteiro JCS, Aredes ND, Bueno JV, Domingues AN, Coutinho VRD, Baptista RCN. (2020). Interdisciplinary simulation scenario in nursing education: Humanized childbirth and birth. Revista Latino-Americana de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.3681.3286
title: High technology is not necessary for successful simulation-based learning
description: The article argues that "the availability of high technology is not necessary to guarantee the success of the activity", citing a Guatemala course with few technological resources conducted in situ with encouraging results, and an in situ study with kindergarten and elementary teachers showing increased self-confidence. It recommends that for institutions without a high-fidelity environment, "conducting the simulation in health units - when available for this purpose - can be an interesting proposal", or using a portable simulator with significantly lower cost, or mixing simulated anatomical parts with an actor representing the patient.
requirements: A portable simulator, an in situ health unit, or a mix of simulated anatomical parts and an actor representing the patient
constraints: Communication with a mannequin is impaired in the non-verbal aspect, which mixed actor-based simulation can strengthen
target_learners: nursing students
teachers in low-resource institutions
target_learning_goals: clinical simulation skills
interpersonal communication in care
examples: A Guatemala simulation course with few technological resources conducted in situ obtained results encouraging simulation use in that context

citation: Wang A, Saltarelli N, Cooper D, Amatya Y, House DR. (2020). Establishing a Low-Resource Simulation Emergency Medicine Curriculum in Nepal. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10924
title: Build low-resource simulation labs from locally available equipment and free software rather than purchased simulators
description: The article demonstrates that a functional simulation lab can be assembled from items a hospital already owns: a CPR manikin, an intubation trainer, and a projector displaying a free cardiac monitor program. The authors state "None of the items were purchased as all were available at Patan Hospital," and that the only contributed resource was free-to-use monitor software. This makes simulation feasible where cost and equipment availability are limiting factors.
requirements: Access to locally available basic equipment such as a manikin, intubation trainer, projector, and computer
constraints: The authors caution that generalizability "may be challenging as local resources may be different" across resource-limited settings
target_learners: Medical officers
Medical students on emergency medicine rotation
target_learning_goals: Emergency medicine case management
Airway management
Teamwork and communication
examples: The Patan Hospital lab used one Resusci Anne manikin, one Ambu intubation trainer, and a free-to-use cardiac monitor program displayed on a projector, with ED supplies such as endotracheal tubes and a bougie

title: Use low-fidelity simulation with simple abstract images for novice learners acquiring basic psychomotor skills
description: The article argues that simulator fidelity should match learner expertise: "for novice learners, low-fidelity models that reproduce the essential constructs of a procedure allow a faster and more cost-effective learning curve to be achieved." Simple images reduce novice confusion when learning basic skills, while experts benefit from higher-fidelity simulations. SIMISGEST-VR therefore adopted a low-fidelity, abstract circular 3D environment for basic psychomotor skills learning.

constraints: Experts benefit from higher-fidelity simulations, so this principle applies to the novice phase of the learning curve
target_learners: novice surgeons
surgery residents

examples: SIMISGEST-VR's environment was redesigned from rectangular to abstract circular shapes, closer to the view of body cavities during MIS, based on expert surgeon feedback

article_title: Design and Evaluation of a Low-Cost Bronchoscopy-Guided Percutaneous Dilatational Tracheostomy Simulator.
citation: Kattan Eduardo MD, MMEd; Vera Magdalena MD; Putz Francisca RN; Corvetto Marcia MD; De la Fuente Rene MD, MScEng; Bravo Sebastian MD. (2019). Design and Evaluation of a Low-Cost Bronchoscopy-Guided Percutaneous Dilatational Tracheostomy Simulator. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000399
title: Low-cost BG-PDT simulator built from hardware-store materials, synthetic skin, bovine tracheas, and a USB pipe inspection camera
description: A simulator for bronchoscopy-guided percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy assembled from a plastic cutting board, PVC pipes, screws, and zip ties, plus synthetic skin pads, ex vivo bovine tracheas, and a flexible pipe inspection camera connected to a laptop to emulate the live bronchoscopic view. It allows multiple uses per assembly: each trachea allowed for 6 iterations and each skin pad for 9, with reassembly for a new use taking 5 minutes. Construction time was 1 hour.
requirements: Materials easily obtained from a hardware store plus synthetic skin pads, ex vivo bovine tracheas, and a 7-mm flexible USB pipe inspection camera
A second operator to manipulate the inspection camera and facilitate the bronchoscopic view
constraints: The simulator could not replicate bleeding, which participants called an important complication of the procedure
Participants noted bovine trachea is a little bit more rigid than human trachea
target_learners: Senior-year anesthesiology or internal medicine residents
Intensive care specialists and residents
target_learning_goals: Bronchoscopy-guided percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy procedural skill
examples: Three iterations were constructed and tested by experts until the final version was obtained, testing adhesive tape and paper clamps to fasten the skin and PVC tubes

Design allowing multiple uses per assembly to keep consumable costs low
constraints: Adding anatomically correct bleeding modules could improve fidelity but also increase building complexity and cost

target_learning_goals: Technical procedural skills training without harm to patients
examples: The BG-PDT simulator was replicated-ready: the authors state it can be easily replicated in any ICU worldwide
